final_message:
All three versions pass every sample, plus 60 randomized small inputs checked against a literal implementation of the recurrence (including zero costs and alphabet sizes 1–26).

**Algorithm (shared by all three):** Two-row DP, but reformulated in "reduced coordinates" `P[j] = Dprev[j] − prefIns[j]`, where `prefIns` is the cumulative insertion cost along the columns. In these coordinates row 0 is all zeros, the up/diagonal candidates are `min(P[j+1] + del, P[j] + sub − ins)`, and the insertion (left) edge becomes a running prefix-minimum along the row. This leaves a dependency-free candidate computation followed by one cheap scan. Pairs are transposed (swapping ins/del and transposing the substitution table) so the row count is the smaller length. The only shortcut is `s == t → 0`, which is always safe since costs are non-negative and the diagonal is 0. I deliberately used no prefix/suffix stripping, banding, or cost-closure tricks: with arbitrary costs (e.g. `del[x]=0`, `sub[a][x]=0`, `ins[b]=0`) those change the answer.

**Per version:**

- [rust/src/main.rs](D:\projects\nb-work\39-rust-vs-python\sessions\wonder-full\align\rust\src\main.rs): hand-written byte scanner (no regex/serde needed), precomputed `sub − ins` rows per alphabet letter, `i32` arithmetic with a generic `i64` fallback when lengths could overflow, iterator-based candidate pass that auto-vectorizes, reused buffers, one buffered output string. [rust/Cargo.toml](D:\projects\nb-work\39-rust-vs-python\sessions\wonder-full\align\rust\Cargo.toml) adds fat LTO and `codegen-units = 1`. Built with `cargo build --release --offline`.
- [plain.py](D:\projects\nb-work\39-rust-vs-python\sessions\wonder-full\align\plain.py): tokenizes with `bytes.split()` and maps letters to indices with `bytes.translate()`; each DP row is a single list comprehension where a walrus variable carries the running minimum (`run := min(run, up+d, diag+sm)`). I microbenchmarked scalar loops, `map`/`accumulate` chains, and `array('i')` variants on real data; this form was fastest.
- [fast.py](D:\projects\nb-work\39-rust-vs-python\sessions\wonder-full\align\fast.py): same row structure as four NumPy passes over preallocated `int32` buffers with `out=` and pre-made slice views (two `add`s, `minimum`, `minimum.accumulate` seeded via the row's first element), `int64` fallback for very long strings.

**Sample results:** all three produce the expected output for s1, s2, and s3 in [samples](D:\projects\nb-work\39-rust-vs-python\sessions\wonder-full\align\samples\s1.out).

**Speed check** on a self-generated input of benchmark shape (300 pairs, ~58M cells; best of 2 runs, machine busy so treat as indicative): Rust ≈ 0.16 s, NumPy ≈ 0.83 s, plain Python ≈ 14 s, all three outputs identical.

request.prompt:
You are writing three versions of the same program, one in Rust and two in Python, for a comparison of how
fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Write these three files:

1. `rust/src/main.rs`: Rust, compiled with rustc 1.99 (edition 2024). The Cargo project in `rust/` is set
   up. The only crates you may use are serde (with derive), serde_json, regex and rayon. They are already
   listed in `rust/Cargo.toml` and vendored, so build offline with `cargo build --release --offline` inside
   `rust/`. Do not add other dependencies. You may change the `[profile.release]` settings in
   `rust/Cargo.toml`.
2. `plain.py`: Python 3.13, standard library only.
3. `fast.py`: Python 3.13, standard library plus NumPy 2.2.

Each program is run with the path of one input file as its argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments). It reads that file and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes. The
Python versions are run as `C:\Python313\python.exe plain.py INPUT_PATH` and
`C:\Python313\python.exe fast.py INPUT_PATH`, and the Rust version as the release binary
`rust/target/release/solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Test all three versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside this
folder, and take at most about 45 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time:
never stop a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example
`taskkill /IM python.exe` or `Stop-Process -Name python`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
